findings.title: Symlinked ownership marker guard remains untested
findings.why_it_matters: The safe fix closes two independent symlink paths, but the regression test exercises only a dangling skill-directory symlink. A future removal of the marker-level `! -L` check would let a third-party skill directory point its ownership marker at installer-owned text and be replaced or deleted without force while this suite still passes.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a fixture with a regular third-party skill directory whose `.mcp-bpmn-installer-owned` file is a symlink to a file containing the ownership marker. Assert install without FORCE rejects it and leaves the directory byte-for-byte intact; also assert uninstall preserves it if removal behavior is in scope.
evidence: tests/install-agent-integrations.test.sh:341-354 covers only a dangling symlink at the skill destination and never creates a symlinked ownership-marker file.
The original security fix explicitly required cases for both dangling destination symlinks and symlinked marker files; only the first case is present.

residual_risks: The WSL checks are automated through lexical `/mnt/<drive>` path simulation and documented for a real WSL2 smoke, but this re-review did not execute the manual smoke in a genuine WSL2 kernel environment.
testing_gaps: The rollback scenarios prove configuration contents are restored, but the fake `cp` wrapper does not record or assert that both snapshot and restore invocations include `-f`; the `cp -pf` policy fix is verified statically rather than by a regression assertion.

The Claude no-force conflict test compares command-substitution strings rather than files with `cmp` and clears the Claude argv log before checking that the refusal made only the read-only `mcp get` call, so its stated byte-for-byte/no-mutation guarantee is slightly stronger than its assertions. The success/failure and final-state regression are covered.
